analysis.one_liner: Repeals oil and gas tax subsidies and redirects the money to hydrogen and fuel cell programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal four tax breaks for the oil and gas industry that were created in the 2005 energy law: a write-off for liquid fuel refinery equipment, faster depreciation for natural gas distribution and gathering lines, expanded depletion deductions for small petroleum refiners, and faster write-offs for geological and geophysical exploration costs [S2] [S3]. The revenue from repealing those breaks would go into a Treasury account for Department of Energy hydrogen and fuel cell research programs [S2] [S3]. The bill was introduced by Representative Albert Wynn in January 2007, referred to four House committees, and never moved again [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, taxpayers would have stopped paying for tax breaks that go to oil refineries and natural gas pipeline owners, and the recovered revenue would have funded federal hydrogen and fuel cell research that the bill describes as previously underfunded [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill terminates the special expensing allowance for liquid fuel refinery equipment created by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, ending a tax break for oil refiners [S2] [S3].

It repeals accelerated depreciation for natural gas distribution and gathering lines and accelerated amortization of geological and geophysical exploration costs, so those oil and gas companies would deduct expenses over the standard timeline instead of faster [S2] [S3].

It narrows the exception that had let small petroleum refiners claim the oil depletion allowance by restoring the 50,000-barrel refinery limit, cutting a deduction for refiners above that size [S2] [S3].

All revenue raised by these repeals would be reserved in the Treasury for Department of Energy hydrogen and fuel cell programs, with priority to programs the bill says were previously underfunded [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners and natural gas pipeline and distribution companies would pay more in taxes by losing the accelerated write-offs and the expanded depletion deduction; their costs could eventually show up in fuel prices, though the bill contains no analysis of that [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners and gas pipeline owners

drawbacks.text: Repealing refinery and pipeline tax breaks could raise costs for oil and gas companies, and the bill provides no estimate or safeguard against those costs being passed to consumers through fuel or heating prices [S2] [S3].

The revenue for hydrogen and fuel cell programs is not guaranteed funding: the money is only available 'to the extent provided in advance in appropriations Acts,' meaning future Congresses would still have to vote each year to spend it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect would be shifting federal money from oil and gas tax breaks to clean energy research. The strongest honest objection is that removing industry write-offs could add to fuel costs, although by how much is unknown, and the clean energy funding would depend on annual appropriations votes rather than being locked in. On balance it would move taxpayer money away from mature, profitable energy industries and toward technology the federal government was underfunding.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees in January 2007 and then to subcommittees, and none of them ever voted on it; the bill died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Representative Albert Wynn of Maryland introduced the bill on January 16, 2007 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and additionally to the Science and Technology, Oversight and Government Reform, and Energy and Commerce Committees [S5].

In early 2007 it was referred to three subcommittees: Energy and Environment (January 31), Energy and Air Quality (February 2), and Government Management, Organization, and Procurement (March 20) [S5].
No further action was ever taken, and no cosponsor ever signed on, so the bill never received a markup or a floor vote and expired at the end of the 110th Congress on January 3, 2009 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the tax breaks the bill would have repealed, and no revenue was redirected to hydrogen and fuel cell programs. Taxpayers continued paying for the subsidies, and the underfunded clean energy programs received nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies kept their tax breaks

against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill; it was referred to his committee and other committees in January 2007 and never advanced.

against.name: House subcommittee chairs
against.role: Chairs of the Energy and Environment, Energy and Air Quality, and Government Management subcommittees
against.what_they_did: Received referrals of the bill in early 2007 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested; the sole sponsor was a Democrat in a Democratic-controlled House, but he attracted no cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Oil refiners and oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill repeals four tax breaks from the 2005 energy law that let refiners and gas companies deduct costs faster and claim larger depletion allowances. Losing those breaks would cost the industry money that would otherwise come from taxpayers.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline and distribution companies
industries.note: Accelerated depreciation for natural gas distribution and gathering lines would be repealed, raising those companies' taxable income.

industries.industry: Hydrogen and fuel cell technology firms
industries.note: The bill reserves the revenue from the tax-break repeals for Department of Energy hydrogen and fuel cell programs, which would fund research benefiting companies in that field, though only if Congress votes the money each year.
